verses.zh: 论到祭偶像之物，我们晓得我们都有知识。但知识是叫人自高自大，惟有爱心能造就人。
verses.en: With regard to food sacrificed to idols, we know that “we all have knowledge.”[NOTE:1] Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
notes: “We all have knowledge.” Here and in v. 4 Paul cites certain slogans the Corinthians apparently used to justify their behavior (cf. 6:12-13; 7:1; 10:23). Paul agrees with the slogans in part, but corrects them to show how the Corinthians have misused these ideas.

verses.zh: 若有人以为自己知道甚么，按他所当知道的，他仍是不知道。
verses.en: If someone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know to the degree that he needs to know.

verses.zh: 若有人爱　神，这人乃是　神所知道的。
verses.en: But if someone loves God, he[NOTE:1] is known by God.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “him”; in the translation the most likely referent (God) has been specified for clarity.

verses.zh: 论到吃祭偶像之物，我们知道偶像在世上算不得甚么，也知道　神只有一位，再没有别的　神。
verses.en: With regard then to eating food sacrificed to idols, we know that “an idol in this world is nothing,” and that “there is no God but one.”[NOTE:1]
notes: “An idol in this world is nothing” and “There is no God but one.” Here and in v. 1 Paul cites certain slogans the Corinthians apparently used to justify their behavior (cf. 6:12-13; 7:1; 10:23). Paul agrees with the slogans in part, but corrects them to show how the Corinthians have misused these ideas.

verses.zh: 虽有称为　神的，或在天，或在地，就如那许多的　神，许多的主；
verses.en: If after all there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many gods and many lords),

verses.zh: 然而我们只有一位　神，就是父―万物都本于他；我们也归于他―并有一位主，就是耶稣基督―万物都是藉着他有的；我们也是藉着他有的。
verses.en: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we live.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “through whom [are] all things and we [are] through him.”

verses.zh: 但人不都有这等知识。有人到如今因拜惯了偶像，就以为所吃的是祭偶像之物。他们的良心既然软弱，也就污秽了。
verses.en: But this knowledge is not shared by all. And some, by being accustomed to idols in former times, eat this food as an idol sacrifice, and their conscience, because it is weak, is defiled.

gr.gloss: a thing sacrificed to an idol

verses.zh: 其实食物不能叫　神看中我们，因为我们不吃也无损，吃也无益。
verses.en: Now food will not bring us close to God. We are no worse if we do not eat and no better if we do.

verses.zh: 只是你们要谨慎，恐怕你们这自由竟成了那软弱人的绊脚石。
verses.en: But be careful that this liberty of yours does not become a hindrance to the weak.

verses.zh: 若有人见你这有知识的，在偶像的庙里坐席，这人的良心若是软弱，岂不放胆去吃那祭偶像之物吗？
verses.en: For if someone weak sees you who possess knowledge dining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience be “strengthened”[NOTE:1] to eat food offered to idols?
notes: Or “built up”; This is the same word used in v. 1b. It is used ironically here: The weak person is “built up” to commit what he regards as sin.

verses.zh: 因此，基督为他死的那软弱弟兄，也就因你的知识沉沦了。
verses.en: So by your knowledge the weak brother or sister,[NOTE:1] for whom Christ died, is destroyed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “the one who is weak…the brother for whom Christ died,” but see note on the word “Christian” in 5:11.
This may be an indirect middle, “destroys himself.”

verses.zh: 你们这样得罪弟兄们，伤了他们软弱的良心，就是得罪基督。
verses.en: If you sin against your brothers or sisters[NOTE:1] in this way and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.
notes: See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:10.

verses.zh: 所以，食物若叫我弟兄跌倒，我就永远不吃肉，免得叫我弟兄跌倒了。
verses.en: For this reason, if food causes my brother or sister to sin, I will never eat meat again, so that I may not cause one of them[NOTE:1] to sin.
notes: Grk “my brother.” Both “my brother or sister” earlier in the verse and “one of them” here translate the same Greek phrase. Since the same expression occurs in the previous line, a pronoun phrase is substituted here to suit English style, which is less tolerant of such repetition.

Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHT TO I CORINTHIANS 8:1-13

- The literary context runs from 1 Cor. 8:1 ‒ 11:1 as the outline above of NJB shows. This context
deals with how believers should relate to pagan culture. Although the freedom in Christ makes all things clean
(i.e., Rom. 14:14,20), all things do not edity the Body.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDIFY

- The question of eating meat offered to idols seems very strange to moderns. But in the context of Paul's
day and the people of Corinth it was a very important issue. Most social gatherings had religious
connotations in Paul's day. Also, the meat that was sold in the marketplaces of Corinth was mostly, though
not all, from one of the heathen temples. It would have been meat sacrificed to an idol. Eating it would be
viewed as

- joining with the idol/god

- worshiping the idol

- supporting the idol with its purchase

- Theologically chapter 8 is parallel to Romans 14:1-15:13. Both of these deal with the complicated and
difficult subject of how a Christian balances his/her freedom in Christ and his/her responsibility in
love to other believers. This chapter was written first.

Gordon Fee, To What End Exegesis?, pp. 105-128, thinks that this context refers
not to just eating food sacrificed to an idol, but to actually attending and participating in the
meal at the idol's temple (which often involved sexual activity as well, cf. 1 Cor. 10:6-22).

Gordon Fee's commentary on 1 Corinthians in the International Commentary Series,
"revised," is one of my favorite exegetical helps on this NT book.

- This chapter also emphasizes that knowledge, even revelatory knowledge, when it is not balanced with
love for others, is only partially true (cf. 1 Cor. 13:1-13).

- I think James D. G. Dunn, Unity and Diversity in the New Testament, p. 319, has a good summary statement.

"He would not stand for Jewish Christians narrowing down Christian
liberty into legalism (Gal. 5:1ff; Phil. 3:2ff); but neither would he stand for Gentile
Christians perverting Christian liberty into license and elitism (Rom. 16:17f;
1 Cor. 5-6; 8-10; cf 2 Thess. 3:6,14f)."

The universal truth is applied in different ways, depending on the need.

- For Paul "the gospel is for all and I must strive to make it known," was the guiding principle! This is
powerfully expressed in his own words in 1 Cor. 9:19-23!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 1 CORINTHIANS 8:1-3

1Now concerning things sacrificed to
idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge makes arrogant, but love edifies.
2If anyone supposes that he knows anything, he has not yet known as he ought to know;
3 but if anyone loves God, he is known by Him.

8:1 "Now concerning things sacrificed to idols" This is another question (i.e., peri dei, cf. 1 Cor. 7:1,25; 8:1; 12:1;
16:1,12, and possibly 15:1) that was asked by the Corinthian church in a letter which the church wrote to Paul, possibly brought by

- Chloe's people (cf. 1 Cor. 1:11)

- Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus (cf. 1 Cor. 16:17)

- another unstated means

Remember, trying to interpret the Bible is like listening to only one side of a phone conversation.
Only history, context, and parallel passages can help.

NASB
"things sacrificed to idols"

NKJV
"things offered to idols"

NRSV
"food sacrificed to idols"

TEV
"food offered to idols"

NJB
"food which has been dedicated to false gods"

Peshitta
"sacrifices offered to idols"

This is a compound term from eidōlon, which means to shape a figure,
image, or statue; and thuō, which means to kill or to offer a sacrifice. This very term was used
to prohibit eating meat offered to an idol in the letter sent to Gentile churches from the Jerusalem
Council in Acts 15:29 (cf. Acts 21:25).

▣ "we know that we all have knowledge" This may be an allusion to the New Covenant of
Jer. 31:31-34, esp. v. 34. Possibly this was

- a quote from the letter that the Corinthian church wrote to Paul

- a slogan of one of the factious groups

- a quote from Paul's earlier preaching, which the Corinthian church had misunderstood

▣ "Knowledge makes arrogant, but love edifies" Paul agrees with the statement, but limits the concept
and shows the true meaning and application (this is also true of the false teachers' slogans in chapters 6-7).

Knowledge was one of the aspects of Greek culture in which some in the Corinthian church
prided themselves. The problem with knowledge is that it tends to make one competitive and prideful
(cf. 1 Cor. 4:6,18,19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4; 2 Cor. 12:20). See full note at 1 Cor. 4:6. It focuses on the
individual, not on the family, the body, the church.

The term "edify" is building imagery. Paul often speaks of "building up" or "edifying"
the church or individual Christians (cf. Rom. 14:19; 15:2; 1 Cor. 8:1; 10:23; 14:3,5,12,26; 2 Cor. 10:8;
12:19; 13:10; Eph. 4:12,29; 1 Thess. 5:11).

Love is crucial in our Christian freedom. Knowledge will not solve the problem of pride;
only self-limiting love can do this. Believers are to pursue that which builds up the church, not that
which glorifies gifted individual Christians. Because a believer can, does not mean he/she should.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDIFY

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIANITY IS CORPORATE

8:2 "If" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE which is assumed
to be true from the author's perspective or for his literary purposes (cf. 1 Cor. 8:3,5). The identification
of these CONDITIONAL SENTENCES is not interpretative, but textual.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII.

▣ "anyone supposes that he knows anything" This is a PERFECT ACTIVE INDICAtive followed
by a PERFECT INFINITIVE. This reflects the settled arrogance of an element/faction of the Corinthian church (cf. 1 Cor. 3:18).

NASB
"he has not yet known as he ought to know"

NKJV, Peshitta
"he knows nothing yet as he ought to know"

NRSV
"does not yet have the necessary knowledge"

TEV
"really don't know as they ought to know"

NJB
"and yet not know it as well as he should"

Paul reveals their lack of spiritual knowledge. Worldly wisdom (i.e., human philosophy)
causes divisions and arrogance, but God's knowledge of us (cf. 1 Cor. 13:12; Gal. 4:9) and our knowledge of
the gospel free us to serve Him and His people (cf. Romans 6).

8:3 "but if anyone loves God" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. There were
those at Corinth who loved God. Notice Paul's emphasis is on love (i.e., PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE),
not on knowledge (cf. 1 Cor. 13:1-13).

▣ "he is known by Him" This may be another example of the slogans of those who claimed to be more
enlightened and spiritual. It is very similar to a later Gnostic phrase found in Gospel of Truth 19.33.
The truly enlightened ones know that there are not divisions between humans, not between

- Jew ‒ Gentile

- slaves ‒ free

- males ‒ females

- strong ‒ weak

All human barriers and distinctives are "removed" in Christ (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; 3:22; 1 Cor. 12:13;
Gal. 3:28; Eph. 3:11-22; 4:6; Col. 3:11)!

Our knowledge of God is important, but knowledge about God is no substitute for a personal
relationship, initiated by God, that issues in our love for one another which expresses our love for Him
(i.e., 2 Tim. 2:19; 1 John 3:14-18; 4:7-21). The great truth is that believers are known by God (cf. Rom. 8:29; Gal. 4:9)!

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 1 CORINTHIANS 8:4-6

4Therefore concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, we know that there
is no such thing as an idol in the world, and that there is no God but one. 5For even if there are so-called gods whether in heaven or
on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords, 6yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom are all things
and we exist for Him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we exist through Him.

8:4 "we know that there is no such thing as an idol in the world" There is a word play on the connotations
in these verses between the Hebrew concept of "know" as personal relationship (cf. 1 Cor. 8:3; Gen. 4:1; Jer. 1:5)
and the Greek connotation of "know" as facts about something or someone (cf. 1 Cor. 8:1,2,4).

In the OT idols were "empty" or "vain." They were not gods at all (cf. 2 Chr. 13:9;
Isa. 37:19; 41:29; Jer. 2:11; Acts 14:15; Gal. 4:8). Paul, later in 1 Corinthians, asserts that demons
use people's superstitions and idolatry (cf. Deut. 32:17; Ps. 106:37; 1 Cor. 10:20; Rev. 9:20), but there is no reality to idols!

Just an added note to clarify, there is no reality to pagan gods, images made by human hands.
However, this does not imply there are other spiritual entities that affect human life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: EMPTY, VAIN, FALSE, NOTHINGNESS

▣ "there is no God but one" This is the theological affirmation of monotheism (cf. 1 Tim. 2:5-6).
According to biblical revelation there is only one true God (cf. 1 Cor. 8:6; Deut. 4:35,39; Ps. 86:8,10). Often
the OT speaks of other "elohim" (i.e., spiritual beings), but none like (i.e., in the same category,
cf. Exod. 20:2-3; Deut. 32:39) as YHWH (cf. Exod. 15:11; Ps. 86:8; 89:6). The Jewish prayer called the Shema
from Deut. 6:4, is the Jewish affirmation quoted daily and at every sabbath worship service asserting the uniqueness
and oneness of YHWH (cf. Mark 12:28-29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D. (YHWH)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. (Elohim)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEMA

8:6 "yet for us there is but one God" This is the theological affirmation of monotheism.
See note at 1 Cor. 8:4.

In the history of religion there have been several categories of beliefs about deity.

- animism, spiritual beings are related to natural processes or objects

- polytheism, the existence of many gods

- henotheism, many gods, but only one god for us (i.e., tribe, nation, geographical area)

- monotheism, the existence of only one God (not the High God of a pantheon)

This text asserts the existence of many spiritual beings (cf. 1 Cor. 8:5), but only one true God
(cf. 1 Cor. 8:4). For those in the Judeo-Christian tradition there is only one creator/redeemer God who
exists in three eternal persons.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

▣ "the Father" This is a wonderful intimate, personal, familial title for Deity. It emphasizes
God's immanence. This aspect of God can only be known by His self-revelation, not human philosophy or discovery.

Although this familial title appears in the OT sparsely (cf. Deut. 32:5-6; Isa. 63:16; 64:8;
Jer. 31:9,20; Hosea 11:3-4; Mal. 1:6; 2:10), it was Jesus, the Son, who fully revealed this astonishing, intimate
analogy (cf. "our Father," Matt. 6:9; 23:9; Eph. 4:6; Abba, Mark 14:36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FATHERHOOD OF GOD

▣ "from whom are all things" This is affirmation of God as creator (cf. Gen. 1:1; Rom. 11:36; 1 Cor. 11:12;
2 Cor. 5:18), but Jesus was His Agent (cf. John 1:3,10; 1 Cor. 8:6; Col. 1:16; Heb. 1:2; 2:10).

▣ "and we exist for Him" God made the world as a stage for humankind to have fellowship
with Himself (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:18). Once the results of human rebellion (cf. Genesis 3) have been overcome in our salvation
and restoration through Christ, we understand our intended purpose. Once the image of God in mankind is restored
through Christ then the intimate, personal fellowship of Eden is restored.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDEN

▣ "one Lord, Jesus Christ" The title "Lord" reflects an OT substitution of Adon for YHWH, which is
a form of the Hebrew VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3:14). The Jews were afraid to pronounce this holy covenant name
lest they take it in vain, therefore, they substituted the Hebrew term Adon or Lord.

Calling Jesus Lord (i.e., kurios is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Adon)
is a way of affirming His Deity and oneness with YHWH (cf. Phil. 2:11). The concept of oneness is also
significant (cf. Eph. 4:5; 1 Tim. 2:5).

Although Paul does not use Theos (i.e., God) for Jesus in this context, he does
use it of Jesus in Acts 20:28; Rom. 9:5; and Titus 2:13 and Theotētus in Col. 2:9. There
can be no doubt that in Paul's mind Jesus is divine. Paul was a strict monotheist. He never qualifies
how one God can eternally exist in three personal manifestations, but that is the obvious conclusion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

▣ "by whom are all things, and we exist through Him" Jesus was the Father's agent in creation
(cf. John 1:3,10; 1 Cor. 8:6; Col. 1:16; Heb. 1:2; 2:10). This was the role of personified wisdom in Proverbs 8:22-31. Wisdom is
FEMININE in Hebrew (cf. Prov. 8:1-21) because the NOUN "wisdom" (BDB 315) is
a FEMININE GENDER NOUN. In this passage we see the tension between our affirmation of monotheism
and the NT revelation of the Trinity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 1 CORINTHIANS 8:7-13

7However not all men have this knowledge; but some, being accustomed to the idol until now, eat food as if it were sacrificed to an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled. 8But food will not commend us to God; we are neither the worse if we do not eat, nor the better if we do eat. 9But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. 10For if someone sees you, who have knowledge, dining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, if he is weak, be strengthened to eat things sacrificed to idols? 11For through your knowledge he who is weak is ruined, the brother for whose sake Christ died. 12And so, by sinning against the brethren and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ. 13Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause my brother to stumble.

8:7 "However not all men have this knowledge" This is a precursor to the "weaker" and "stronger"
Christian developed in Rom. 14:1,2,14,22-23; 15:1. "Weak" in this context refers to superstition or legalism
connected with one's past, pre-converted life. This is a sarcastic glance back to 1 Cor. 8:1 and the arrogance
of certain factions of the church of Corinth and their emphasis on wisdom and knowledge (cf. 1 Cor. 8:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN FREEDOM vs. CHRISTIAN RESPONSIBILITY

▣ "and their conscience being weak is defiled" Believers must act in faith on the light we have
(cf. Rom. 14:23), even when this knowledge is erroneous or spiritually childish. Believers are only responsible
for what they do understand.

Paul uses the term "conscience" often in the Corinthian letters (cf. 1 Cor. 4:4; 8:7,10,12; 1
0:25,27,28,29; 2 Cor. 1:12; 4:2; 5:11). It refers to that moral inner sense of what is appropriate or
inappropriate (cf. Acts 23:1). The conscience can be affected by our past lives, our poor choices, the demonic, or by
the Spirit of God. It is not a flawless guide, but it does determine the boundaries of individual faith.
Therefore, to violate our conscience, even if it is in error or weak, is a major faith problem (cf. Rom. 14:23).

The believer's conscience needs to be more and more formed by the Word of God and the Spirit of
God (cf. 1 Tim. 3:9). God will judge believers by the light they have (i.e., weak or strong), but all of us need
to be open to the Bible and the Spirit for more light and to be growing in the knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ.
See fuller note on "conscience" at 1 Cor. 10:25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSCIENCE

▣ "defiled" This term originally referred to unclean clothing (cf. Zech. 3:3-4; Jude 23; Rev. 3:4).
It came to be used figuratively for moral pollution (cf. Rev. 14:4; also note Eph. 4:22,24,25,31).

It is surprising that this term is chosen to describe what happens to weak believers who violate
their own faith boundaries. God looks at the heart in every situation. Breaking our faith understanding, even
if weak or inappropriate, is a serious breach of faith (cf. Rom. 14:23)!

8:8 "But food will not commend us to God" This shows the faulty theology, both of those who affirm
asceticism, or Jewish legalism, as well as those who affirm radical freedom. Neither eating or not eating
will present us acceptable to God (cf. Rom. 14:14,23; Mark 7:18-23). Love for God expressed in self-limiting
love for other brothers and sisters in Christ is the key to peace and maturity within the Christian fellowship (i.e., Eph. 4:1-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: OT FOOD LAWS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

▣ "commend" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOUND

▣ "if. . .if" There are two THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL PHRASES in 1 Cor. 8:8, which show potential action.

8:9

NASB, NRSV
"But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow

become a stumbling block to the weak"

NKJV
"But beware lest somehow this liberty of yours becomes

a stumbling block to those who are weak"

TEV
"Be careful, however, not to let your freedom of action make

those who are weak in the faith fall into sin"

NJB
"Only be careful that this freedom of yours does not in anyway

turn into an obstacle to trip those who are vulnerable"

This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE. Christian freedom (i.e., exousia,
cf. 1 Cor. 9:4,5,6,12,18) must be controlled by love or it becomes a license (cf. 1 Cor. 10:23-33; 13:1-13;
Rom. 14:1-15:13).

The classical passage on the subject of Christian freedom and responsibility is in Rom. 14:1-15:13. We are our brother's keeper!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN FREEDOM vs. CHRISTIAN RESPONSIBILITY

8:10 "if" This is another THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL which means potential action.
The grammar of 1 Cor. 8:10 expects a "yes" answer.

NASB, NKJV
"someone sees you, who have knowledge, dining in an idol's temple"

NRSV
"others see you who possess knowledge, eating in the temple of an idol"

TEV
"Suppose a person whose conscience is weak in this matter, sees you,

who have so-called 'knowledge' eating in the temple of an idol"

NJB
"Suppose someone sees you who have the knowledge,

sitting in the temple of some false god"

This phrase is translated ambiguously in NASB and NKJV. The idiomatic, dynamic equivalent
translations of TEV and NJB capture the thought.

The knowledge Paul is referring to goes back to 1 Cor. 8:1-4. Strong believers know that there
is only one God (cf. 1 Cor. 8:4). Weak believers are still influenced by the past. Strong believers bend over
backwards so as not to offend their weak brothers or sisters in Christ or sincere seekers (cf. Rom. 14:1,15; 15:1; 1 Cor. 8:1).

True spiritual strength is not in knowledge only, but in loving actions toward other believers,
even weak ones, superstitious ones, legalistic ones, ascetic ones, baby ones! True knowledge makes one a humble
steward of the undeserved grace of God in Christ (i.e., Gal. 6:2)!

▣ "dining in an idol's temple" See notes at 1 Cor. 10:14-22.

NASB
"be strengthened"

NKJV
"be emboldened to eat"

NRSV
"be encouraged to the point of eating"

TEV, Peshitta
"will not this encourage him to eat"

NJB
"may be encouraged to eat"

This is the term "build up" or "edify" as in verse 1. Here it is used in either

- a sarcastic sense about the destructive influence of the stronger brother's actions

- a possible quote from the Corinthian letter related to how to help those with weak faith

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDIFY

8:11

NASB
"For through your knowledge he who is weak is ruined,

the brother for whose sake Christ died"

NKJV
"And because of your knowledge shall the weak brother perish,

for whom Christ died"

NRSV
"So by your knowledge those weak believers

for whom Christ died are destroyed"

TEV
"And so this weak person, your brother for whom Christ died,

will perish because of your 'knowledge'"

NJB
"And then it would be through your knowledge that this brother

for whom Christ died, vulnerable as he is, has been lost"

The order of the Greek sentence emphasizes "your" (i.e., this so called superior knowledge
you possess). When one Christian's freedom destroys another Christian, that freedom is a disaster (cf. Rom. 14:15,20).

This is a sarcastic comment as is 1 Cor. 8:10. The Corinthian church was proud of their knowledge (1 Cor. 5:2; 8:1).
Here Paul shows knowledge can be a disaster. Paul always admonishes the "stronger" brother to have patience and concern
for the "weaker" brother, because of Christ's love for them both.

The terms "ruined," "perish," or "destroyed" must be interpreted in light of Rom. 14:22-23,
where it means "causing another to sin," which is analogous to the use of the term here. This is not ultimate
destruction, but a temporary, yet serious, set-back in spiritual growth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN FREEDOM vs. CHRISTIAN RESPONSIBILITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESTRUCTION (apollumi)

8:12 "by sinning against the brethren. . .you sin against Christ" This is a powerful statement. Our love
for God is shown in our love for one another (cf. 1 John 4:7-21). Several times in the NT,

- people's actions against believers are seen as actions against Christ (cf. Acts 9:4,5)

- people's actions for believers are seen as actions for Christ (cf. Matt. 25:40,45)

8:13 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. Food issues were causing some believers
to violate their personal faith assumptions.

▣ "stumble" This is the Greek term that was used of trapping animals. Literally it referred to "a baited trap-stick."

▣ "I will never eat meat again" This verse has a very strong triple NEGATIVE
construction (cf. Rom. 14:21). Freedom in Christ should edify, not destroy. The unstated implication is that
Paul will not eat meat sacrificed to an idol or in an idol's temple. This does not imply that Paul became a vegetarian.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- It is obvious that this particular problem in not a contemporary one; however, the universal principle
here is very significant. State that principle in your own words.

- How does one relate demon activity to world religions in our day?

- If there is only one God, how can Jesus be divine?

- Explain the relationship between Christian freedom and Christian responsibility.

- Define "weak" and "strong" believers.

- Should all believers be vegetarians?
